query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of refractory elements, such as Molybdenum (Mo) and Tungsten (W), to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with a composition of 5-35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii.
generation.intervention: The addition of refractory elements, such as Molybdenum (Mo) and Tungsten (W), to the alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a single-phase solid solution with a face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure.
generation.mechanism: The refractory elements will enhance the solid solution strengthening effect, leading to improved mechanical properties at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy will exhibit improved strength, hardness, and resistance to oxidation and corrosion at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties of the alloy without the addition of refractory elements.
generation.boundary: The alloy's composition and processing conditions, such as the cooling rate and heat treatment.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount and combination of refractory elements to add to the alloy, as well as the potential effects on the alloy's microstructure and properties.

falsification_experiment.design: A comparative study of the mechanical properties of the alloy with and without the addition of refractory elements at elevated temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with the addition of refractory elements does not exhibit improved mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites []. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new materials that can overcome the limitations of the existing physical properties, and many studies are being conducted on them intensively []. General alloys are composed of the main element and a small number of substituted elements. In these alloys, as the number of constituent elements increases, intermetallic compounds are formed, and the mechanical properties are weakened, owing to their brittleness. HEAs are composed of 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii []. In this case, they exhibit high configurational entropy, severe lattice distortion, and a slow diffusion rate.
